cards.title: Problem 1 · Algebra
cards.stem: Find all polynomials $P(x)$ with real coefficients such that $$P(x^2-2)=P(x)^2-2\qquad\text{for all real }x.$$

key.rationale:
Answer. The constants $P\equiv2$ and $P\equiv-1$, and for each $n\ge1$ the polynomial $P_n$ given by $$P_0=2,\quad P_1=x,\quad P_{k+1}=xP_k-P_{k-1}\qquad(\text{so }P_2=x^2-2,\ P_3=x^3-3x,\ \dots),$$ which is characterised by $P_n\!\left(t+\tfrac1t\right)=t^n+t^{-n}$, equivalently $P_n(2\cos\theta)=2\cos n\theta$.

Constants. $P\equiv c$ works iff $c=c^2-2$, i.e. $c\in\{2,-1\}$.

Leading coefficient. Let $\deg P=n\ge1$ with leading coefficient $c$. Comparing the coefficients of $x^{2n}$ gives $c=c^2$, so $c=1$.

Uniqueness in each degree. Suppose $P\ne Q$ both satisfy the equation and both have degree $n\ge1$. Let $R=P-Q\ne0$, of degree $m\lt n$ (both are monic). Subtracting the two equations, $$R(x^2-2)=P(x)^2-Q(x)^2=R(x)\,\bigl(P(x)+Q(x)\bigr).$$ The left side has degree $2m$. On the right, $P+Q$ has leading term $2x^n$, so the degree is $m+n$. Then $2m=m+n$ gives $m=n$, a contradiction. So for each $n\ge1$ there is at most one solution of degree $n$.

Existence. By induction, $P_n$ is a monic polynomial of degree $n$ with real coefficients and $P_n(t+t^{-1})=t^n+t^{-n}$ for all $t\ne0$. This holds for $n=0,1$, and $$(t+t^{-1})(t^k+t^{-k})-(t^{k-1}+t^{1-k})=t^{k+1}+t^{-k-1}.$$ For $x=t+t^{-1}$ we have $x^2-2=t^2+t^{-2}$, so $$P_n(x^2-2)=t^{2n}+t^{-2n}=(t^n+t^{-n})^2-2=P_n(x)^2-2 .$$ As $t$ ranges over $[1,\infty)$, $x$ takes every value in $[2,\infty)$. The two polynomials $P_n(x^2-2)$ and $P_n(x)^2-2$ agree at infinitely many points, so they are identical.

By uniqueness, $P_n$ is the only solution of degree $n$. Together with the constants $2$ and $-1$, this is the complete list. $\blacksquare$

rubric.desc: Finds the constant solutions $2$ and $-1$.
Shows that a non-constant solution is monic.
Proves that there is at most one solution of each degree $n\ge1$ (e.g. via $R(x^2-2)=R(x)(P+Q)$ and a degree comparison).
Exhibits a solution of every degree (Chebyshev-type $P_n$ with $P_n(t+1/t)=t^n+t^{-n}$ or $P_n(2\cos\theta)=2\cos n\theta$) and proves it works.
Justifies the identity for all real $x$ (polynomial identity) and states the complete answer. (Listing $x,\ x^2-2,\ x^3-3x$ without the general family: at most 3 total for the answer.)

cards.title: Problem 2 · Number Theory
cards.stem: Find all positive integers $n$ with the following property: for every positive divisor $d$ of $n$, the number $d+2$ divides $n+2$.

key.rationale:
Answer. $n=1$ and all primes $n\equiv1\pmod 3$.

These work. For $n=1$ the only divisor is $1$, and $3\mid3$. For a prime $p\equiv1\pmod3$ the divisors are $1$ and $p$: $3\mid p+2$, and $p+2\mid p+2$.

Necessity for primes. Taking $d=1$ always gives $3\mid n+2$, i.e. $n\equiv1\pmod 3$. In particular a prime solution must be $\equiv1\pmod3$.

No composite solutions. Let $n$ be composite with smallest prime factor $p$, and put $m=n/p$. Then $m\gt 1$ and every prime factor of $m$ is at least $p$, so $m\ge p$. Taking $d=m$: $$m+2\ \Big|\ (n+2)-p(m+2)=2-2p,\qquad\text{so}\qquad m+2\mid 2p-2 .$$ Here $2p-2\gt 0$, and $2(m+2)\ge2p+4\gt 2p-2$. So the quotient $\frac{2p-2}{m+2}$ is a positive integer less than $2$, hence $m+2=2p-2$, i.e. $m=2(p-2)$.

Since $m\gt 1$ we get $p\ge3$, and then $2\mid m\mid n$. This contradicts $p$ being the smallest prime factor of $n$ (it would have to be $2$). So no composite $n$ works. $\blacksquare$

rubric.desc: Verifies that $n=1$ and primes $p\equiv1\pmod 3$ satisfy the condition.
Uses $d=1$ to get $n\equiv1\pmod3$, which settles the prime case.
For composite $n$, chooses a good divisor (e.g. $d=n/p$ with $p$ the least prime factor) and derives $n/p+2\mid 2p-2$.
Uses size ($n/p\ge p$) to force $n/p+2=2p-2$.
Reaches a contradiction (parity / minimality of $p$), completing the proof that composites fail.

cards.title: Problem 3 · Combinatorics
cards.stem:
Let $n\ge3$ be an integer. There are $n$ lamps arranged around a circle, and initially exactly one of them is on. A move consists of choosing a lamp that is on and toggling each of its two neighbours (on becomes off and off becomes on). The chosen lamp itself does not change.

Determine all $n$ for which it is possible, after finitely many moves, to have all $n$ lamps on.

key.rationale:
Answer. Exactly the odd $n$.

Number the lamps $0,1,\dots,n-1$ around the circle (indices mod $n$), with lamp $0$ on initially.

$n$ even is impossible. Colour the lamps alternately white (even index) and black (odd index), which is consistent around the circle because $n$ is even. A move at lamp $i$ toggles lamps $i-1$ and $i+1$, which have the same colour. So the number of lit lamps of each colour changes by $-2$, $0$ or $+2$, and the parity of the number of lit white lamps and of lit black lamps never changes. Initially $1$ white and $0$ black lamps are lit. With all lamps on, $n/2$ lamps of each colour are lit, so we would need $n/2$ to be both odd and even. Impossible.

$n$ odd is possible. Call a set of $L$ consecutive lit lamps, with all other lamps off, a block of length $L$. The initial position is a block of length $1$.

Claim. If the lit lamps form the block $a,a+1,\dots,a+L-1$ with $L$ odd and $L\le n-2$, then the moves at lamps $a,a+2,a+4,\dots,a+L-1$ (in this order) turn it into the block $a-1,a,\dots,a+L$ of length $L+2$.

Proof. Only lamps $a+1,a+3,\dots,a+L-2$ and $a-1,a+L$ are toggled. The chosen lamps $a,a+2,\dots,a+L-1$ are never toggled, so each is still on when chosen and every move is legal. Each lamp $a+2t+1$ ($0\le t\le\frac{L-3}2$) lies between two chosen lamps and is toggled twice, so it ends on. Lamps $a-1$ and $a+L$ are toggled once each and come on. Since $L+2\le n$, these are distinct lamps outside the old block. $\square$

Starting from the block $\{0\}$ and applying the claim with $L=1,3,5,\dots,n-2$, we reach a block of length $n$, i.e. all lamps on. (This uses $1+2+\dots+\frac{n-1}2=\frac{n^2-1}8$ moves.) $\blacksquare$

rubric.desc: Correct answer: all odd $n$.
Impossibility for even $n$ via a complete invariant (parity of lit lamps in each of the two alternate classes).
General construction for every odd $n$ (e.g. growing a block of consecutive lit lamps by $2$). Construction for small cases only: up to 2.
Verifies legality of the construction (chosen lamps are on; toggled lamps end correctly; no overlap when $L\le n-2$).

cards.title: Problem 4 · Geometry

figs.cap: Γ is the circumcircle of ABC and ω is the circle with diameter AD.

cards.stem:
Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $AB\neq AC$ and circumcircle $\Gamma$, and let $D$ be the foot of the altitude from $A$. The circle $\omega$ with diameter $AD$ meets the sides $AB$, $AC$ again at $X$, $Y$ respectively, and meets $\Gamma$ again at $P\neq A$.

Prove that the lines $BC$, $XY$ and $AP$ pass through a common point $T$, and that $TD^2=TB\cdot TC$.

key.rationale:
Step 1: $B,C,Y,X$ are concyclic. Since $AD$ is a diameter of $\omega$, $\angle AXD=90^\circ$, so $X$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $D$ to $AB$. It lies on side $AB$ because the angles at $A$ and $B$ are acute. In the right triangle $ABD$ (right angle at $D$), $DX$ is the altitude to the hypotenuse, so $AX\cdot AB=AD^2$. Similarly $AY\cdot AC=AD^2$. Hence $AX\cdot AB=AY\cdot AC$, and by the converse of the power of a point (with $X\in AB$, $Y\in AC$) the points $B,C,Y,X$ lie on a circle $\sigma$.

Step 2: $XY\not\parallel BC$. From the cyclic quadrilateral $BCYX$, $\angle AXY=\angle ACB$. If $XY\parallel BC$, then $\angle AXY=\angle ABC$, so $\angle B=\angle C$ and $AB=AC$, which is excluded. Let $T=XY\cap BC$.

Step 3: radical axes. Consider the three circles $\Gamma$, $\omega$, $\sigma$:

  • $\Gamma\cap\sigma=\{B,C\}$, so their radical axis is line $BC$;
  • $\omega\cap\sigma=\{X,Y\}$, so their radical axis is line $XY$;
  • $\Gamma\cap\omega=\{A,P\}$, so their radical axis is line $AP$.

The point $T$ lies on the first two radical axes, so it has equal power with respect to all three circles. Hence it lies on the third, line $AP$. So $BC$, $XY$, $AP$ concur at $T$.

Step 4: $TD^2=TB\cdot TC$. The radius of $\omega$ through $D$ is along $AD\perp BC$, so $\omega$ is tangent to $BC$ at $D$. The power of $T$ with respect to $\omega$ is therefore $TD^2$. Note $T\ne D$: $D,X,Y$ are three distinct points of $\omega$, so they are not collinear. With respect to $\Gamma$, the power of $T$ is the signed product $\overline{TB}\cdot\overline{TC}$. By Step 3 the two powers are equal, so $\overline{TB}\cdot\overline{TC}=TD^2\gt 0$. Hence $T$ lies outside segment $BC$ and $TD^2=TB\cdot TC$. $\blacksquare$

rubric.desc: Proves $AX\cdot AB=AD^2=AY\cdot AC$ (or the equivalent angle fact that $XY$ is antiparallel to $BC$).
Concludes that $B,C,Y,X$ are concyclic.
Shows $XY$ is not parallel to $BC$ (uses $AB\ne AC$).
Radical axis argument for the three circles $\Gamma,\omega,\sigma$, giving the concurrence.
Notes that $\omega$ is tangent to $BC$ at $D$.
Deduces $TD^2=TB\cdot TC$ from equal powers.
